newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Afghanistan's young Taleban chief shuns limelight.
newsitem.headline: Afghanistan's young Taleban chief shuns limelight.

text.p: Revered by his men as Amir al-Mumineen (Commander of the Faithful), the Afghan Taleban's youthful leader has kept a low public profile even after his bearded Islamist warriors seized Kabul last month.
Mullah Mohammad Omar, 32, launched the Taleban movement of religious students in the southern province of Kandahar in 1994.
The reclusive leader has not emerged from his Kandahar headquarters to share in the triumph of his fighters who routed other factions to conquer the Afghan capital on September 27.
Omar was born in the central province of Uruzgan and studied in several Islamic madrassahs, or schools, before joining the Jihad (holy war) against the Soviet occupation in the 1980s.
He rose to deputy chief commander in the guerrilla party Harakat-i-Inqilab-i-Islami of Mohammad Nabi Mohammadi during the war, in which he was wounded and lost one eye.
In April 1996, an assembly of about 1,000 Moslem clergymen chose him as Amir al-Momineen, denouncing President Burhanuddin Rabbani as unfit to lead an Islamic nation.
Assisted by a council of religious scholars, Omar wants to get rid of "corrupt" guerrilla factions and impose a strict version of Islamic Sharia law throughout Afghanistan.
Here are brief biographies of other Afghan leaders:
-- Burhanuddin Rabbani, the ousted Afghan president, leads the Jamiat-i-Islami party, which was probably the largest of the factions which fought against Soviet occupation.

An ethnic Tajik from the mountainous northeastern province of Badakhshan and a former professor of Islamic law at Kabul University, he became president in late 1992 for an interim period but extended his term and antagonised most other parties.
-- Ahmad Shah Masood is a former defence minister and Rabbani's army chief, known as the "Lion of Panjsher" for his exploits against Soviet forces in his Panjsher Valley redoubt.
He played a key role in the guerrilla takeover in April 1992 by moving his forces into Kabul after striking an alliance with former communist northern General Abdul Rashid Dostum.

Masood won renown as the strongest Afghan guerrilla leader against the Soviets and was Rabbani's strongman. He withdrew to Panjsher as Kabul fell, but has since driven the Taleban back to the Bagram area, 50 km (30 miles) north of the capital.

-- General Abdul Rashid Dostum is a former pro-communist Uzbek chief whose defection to the mujahideen guerrillas played a key role in the collapse of the communist government in 1992. He leads the Jumbish-i-Milli movement based in the north.

With his own army and a small air force, he controls six northern provinces. He joined then prime minister Gulbuddin Hekmatyar in January 1994 in a failed bid to drive Rabbani and Masood out of Kabul, starting a destructive round of fighting.

He stayed out of the conflict between the Taleban and the Kabul government, while continuing to oppose Rabbani. In September, he struck an informal truce with Rabbani to allow the reopening of the Salang Pass that links Kabul with the north.
-- Gulbuddin Hekmatyar, 45, leads Hezb-i-Islami, once the most disciplined of the anti-Soviet guerrilla groups.
Dynamic and outspoken, Hekmatyar, from the northern province of Kunduz, became involved in Islamic politics at Kabul University's engineering faculty in 1968.
He was jailed for 18 months under then king Zahir Shah and then fought against President Mohammad Daoud's republican government before fleeing into exile in Pakistan in 1974.

Hekmatyar was prime minister from March 1993 until January 1994, when he allied himself with Dostum in the failed coup to oust Rabbani. He was appointed to the same position last June under a peace pact with Rabbani that was opposed by Dostum.

-- Younus Khalis, 74, is a maulvi (religious scholar) and Pashtu poet from the eastern province of Nangarhar who leads his own Hezb-i-Islami (Khalis) faction which he formed after fleeing to Pakistan in 1975 and splitting with Hekmatyar.
Sporting a distinctive beard dyed orange with henna, he declared support for the Taleban last month.
-- Abdurrab Rasul Sayyaf, a former professor of Islamic law at Kabul University, leads the pro-Rabbani Ittehad-i-Islami.
Sayyaf, a fluent Arabic speaker who had close contacts with Saudi Arabia during the anti-Soviet struggle, worked for the Islamic movement in the days of Zahir Shah and Daoud.
He was arrested in the communist takeover of 1978 despite being a relative of Hafizullah Amin, the communist party leader killed during the Soviet intervention next year.
-- Mohammad Nabi Mohammadi, an elderly maulvi and former member of parliament, leads Harakat-i-Inqilab-i-Islami.
It became the largest faction soon after the Soviet intervention because of his influence among conservative clergy. He took no sides between Rabbani and his opponents.

-- Sibghatullah Mojadidi, 70, is a scion of a leading Afghan family and heads Jabha-i-Nijat-i-Milli. He became Afghanistan's first interim Islamic president in April 1992, giving way to Rabbani three months later. His family has close ties with ex-king Zahir Shah and has campaigned for his return.

-- Syed Ahmad Gailani, the most Westernised of the Afghan party leaders, heads Mahaz-i-Milli-i-Islami and has tried to mobilise support for a return of Zahir Shah. Like Mojadidi, he belongs to one of Afghanistan's aristocratic families and has been neutral in the current factional fighting.
-- Karim Khalili leads the the minority Shi'ite Moslem Hezb-i-Wahdat faction based in the central province of Bamiyan.
